blocks.content: Explaining a complex workflow in plain text is like reading assembly instructions without the pictures. The words are all there but nothing quite clicks.
What you need is a visual. In UML that visual is an Activity Diagram.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245798029-a59228cc.png
An Activity Diagram traces the path a process takes from beginning to end every step, every decision, every fork in the road all laid out in one clean picture.

Where sequence diagrams are about objects talking to each other, activity diagrams are about what gets done and in what order. Same idea as a flowchart, but with the vocabulary and structure to handle real-world complexity.
1. What is an Activity Diagram?
An Activity Diagram is a UML diagram that gives a workflow a visual shape. It captures:

["Every action that needs to happen and the order they happen in","The points where a choice sends the flow down different roads","The tasks that do not need to wait for each other and can run together","Who owns which step through the use of swimlanes"]
items: Every action that needs to happen and the order they happen in
The points where a choice sends the flow down different roads
The tasks that do not need to wait for each other and can run together
Who owns which step through the use of swimlanes

blocks.content: Why Activity Diagrams Are Worth Learning
blocks.text: Why Activity Diagrams Are Worth Learning

blocks.content: A workflow that sounds perfectly clear when you describe it out loud has a funny way of falling apart the moment someone else tries to follow it.

Put the entire flow in one place Steps, forks, loops, parallel tracks spreading these across a document or a conversation means people will always miss something. An activity diagram compresses the whole thing onto one canvas. Every path is visible. Every outcome is traceable.

Uncover hidden efficiency Drawing a workflow out has a way of revealing things you never noticed. Two steps you always assumed had to happen in sequence turn out to have no dependency at all. Diagrams make these wins obvious. They also highlight the chokepoints where everything funnels through a single step.

Speak two languages at once A business requirement says "process the student enrollment." A developer writes if (seats.available()) { student.enroll(); }. Neither one makes complete sense to the other side. An activity diagram translates between the two.
2. Components of an Activity Diagram
Every activity diagram uses the same handful of symbols. Get comfortable with these and no diagram will feel unfamiliar.
1. Initial Node
The entry point. One per diagram, always. Drawn as a solid black circle with arrows flowing only outward.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245798260-430b4b30.png
2. Action Node
One task. One responsibility. Drawn as a rounded rectangle with a verb-noun label.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245798330-9a68b402.png
The name tells you exactly what the step does. Vague labels create confusion.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245798409-9deda4b3.jpg
One action per node. The moment a label contains "and" it needs to be two nodes.
3. Final Node
The exit point. A filled circle wrapped inside a larger ring. The instant flow reaches it everything stops.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245798513-f0108737.png
You can have more than one final node a success exit and a rejection exit for example but landing on any one of them brings the whole activity to a halt.
4. Flow Final Node
Shuts down one specific branch without touching anything else. Drawn as a circle with an X.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245798724-14c62fb2.png
The rejected path closes. The admission process carries on as normal.
5. Decision Node
A diamond that sends the flow one way or another based on a condition. Each exit arrow must carry a label.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245798836-ccd04efb.png
Unlabeled exit arrows are a red flag. If the condition is not written down nobody reading the diagram will know which path means what.
6. Merge Node
Gathers separate branches back into a single path. Also a diamond but arrows flow in from multiple directions and out through just one.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245798938-d75c26c7.png
Skip the merge and your branched paths keep spreading outward like a tree with no trunk.
7. Fork Node
Breaks one flow into several parallel flows that all launch simultaneously.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245799089-53999595.png
The moment admission is confirmed all three tasks fire at once. None of them sits around waiting for the others.
8. Join Node
Collects all parallel branches and holds them until every single one has finished. Only then does the flow continue.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245799172-1c17f0ab.png

Orientation does not begin until the welcome email is sent, the classroom is assigned, and the student ID is created. A fork without a matching join is a workflow that branches out and never comes back together almost always a mistake.
3. Control Flow
Components are the vocabulary. Control flow is the grammar how you wire components together to model real behavior. There are four fundamental patterns.
1. Sequential Flow
The simplest pattern. One action finishes, the next one starts. No branching, no waiting, just a straight line from top to bottom.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245799260-47f9bdf1.png

A basic student admission flow. Submit, review, interview, offer, enroll. Each step waits for the previous one before it begins. Start here and add complexity only where the process genuinely needs it.
2. Conditional Flow
The path splits at a decision node and reunites at a merge node. Exactly one branch runs never both.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245799343-dff6092d.png
After verifying documents either the application gets approved or missing documents are requested. The merge pulls both outcomes back into one path. Only one branch ever fires.
3. Parallel Flow
Multiple tasks launch at the same time after a fork and a join waits for all of them before moving on.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245799442-7018f5fb.png
The moment admission is confirmed three things fire simultaneously welcome email, classroom assignment, and student ID creation. Orientation only begins once all three are done.
4. Loop Flow
A branch routes the flow back to an earlier step and keeps repeating until a condition is finally met.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245799583-f9bc8f1e.png

The student submits their application. If eligible they proceed straight to admission. If not they can choose to reapply next term and the loop starts again. If they decide not to reapply a rejection letter goes out and the flow ends.
4. Functional Lanes
So far our diagrams show what happens but not who does it. Swimlanes divide the diagram into lanes one per actor or system so responsibility for every action is immediately obvious.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245799788-807391a8.png
Every arrow crossing a lane boundary is a handoff a moment where one team hands responsibility to another. These crossing points are where most real-world delays and miscommunications happen.
Swimlanes give you several things at once:

["Clear ownership no ambiguity about who handles what","Handoff visibility every boundary crossing is an integration point worth examining","Workload balance a lane with ten actions next to one with two flags an imbalance","Implementation guidance each lane often maps directly to a service, a team, or a module"]
items: Clear ownership no ambiguity about who handles what
Handoff visibility every boundary crossing is an integration point worth examining
Workload balance a lane with ten actions next to one with two flags an imbalance
Implementation guidance each lane often maps directly to a service, a team, or a module

blocks.content: 5. How to Draw an Activity Diagram
blocks.text: 5. How to Draw an Activity Diagram

blocks.content: Step 1: Name the process
Be specific about what you are modeling. "Student admission" beats "the system." The tighter the scope the cleaner the diagram.
Step 2: List every action

Write down every step in rough order without worrying about structure yet. For student admission: submit application, verify documents, schedule interview, check eligibility, send offer, generate invoice, confirm payment, create ID, assign credentials.
Step 3: Arrange in sequence
Order the steps chronologically. Which one must finish before the next can start? This gives you the backbone of the diagram.
Step 4: Find the decision points
Where does the flow branch? Eligible or not eligible. Documents complete or incomplete. Each condition becomes a decision node with labeled exits.
Step 5: Find the parallel steps
Which actions have no dependency on each other? Creating a student ID and sending a welcome email do not need to happen one after the other. These become fork and join pairs.
Step 6: Add swimlanes
If more than one actor or system is involved, divide the diagram into lanes. Optional for simple flows but essential for anything with handoffs between teams.
6. Complete Example: Student Admission Process

Let's build a full activity diagram for a university admission system. It naturally contains all four control flow patterns sequential steps, conditional branching, a retry loop, and parallel execution.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245799900-acb57eda.png
Let's walk through each section.

Document verification sequential + loop The student submits their application and documents get verified. If anything is missing the office requests the outstanding items and the student resubmits. This loop runs until everything is in order.

Interview and eligibility conditional Once documents are complete the interview takes place. If the student does not meet the criteria a rejection letter goes out and the flow ends. If they pass an offer letter is sent.
Payment loop The student pays the admission fee. If the payment fails they retry. The loop continues until a valid payment lands.

Post-admission setup parallel Once admission is confirmed three things happen simultaneously a welcome email goes out, a student ID is created, and a course schedule is assigned. Orientation only begins once all three are done. Running them in parallel cuts the setup time to the length of the slowest task instead of the sum of all three.
